extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics and classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, historical-account chapter discussing Greek treatments of cubic equations, classification of problems (plane/solid/linear), methods (use of conics, exhaustion), and debates (Pappus vs Zeuthen). Useful for understanding ancient geometric criteria and solution methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus' classification of problems (plane / solid / linear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus distinguishes problems which are plane (ἐπίπεδα), solid (στερεά) and linear (γραμμικοί), with a parallel distinction between plane loci, solid loci (conic sections), and linear loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a classificatory standard: Pappus implies problems were called plane/solid/linear because they required loci of the corresponding kind. The text discusses logical defects in this account and how the terms may instead reflect algebraic degree (plane → ≤2, solid → 3, linear → >3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane problem criterion (Pappus' wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Problems which can be solved by means of the straight line and circle may properly be called plane (λέγοισ' ἂν εἰκότως ἐπίπεδα) ; for the lines by means of which such problems are solved have their origin in a plane."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted more precisely: 'plane problems' are those reducible to simple equations between areas (algebraically degree not higher than the second). The chapter argues Pappus' given origin-based explanation is unsatisfactory and that the algebraic-degree reading is more natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid problem criterion (Pappus / Zeuthen debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally 'solid problem' was applied to problems solvable by conics (solid loci); Zeuthen hypothesizes the term refers to problems reducible to cubic equations (simple relations between volumes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two senses are discussed: (a) solid problems as problems reducible to cubic equations (equations between volumes), and (b) solid problems as those solvable by conics regardless of algebraic degree (Pappus' broader usage, which ultimately prevailed). The text weighs historical evidence (Archimedes, Menaechmus, Aristaeus) and finds only partial support for Zeuthen's narrower hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear problem criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'linear' problem/ locus denotes cases equivalent to algebraic equations of an order higher than the third, which do not admit reduction to simple relations between lengths, areas and volumes and require new classes of curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the term may have arisen later and that 'linear' problems were those where 'recourse was had to new classes of curves, directly and without any intermediate step in the shape of an equation.' Examples include the conchoid and cissoid and other higher-order loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' method of exhaustion (standards of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes' extensions of the method of exhaustion avoid using 'infinitely great' or 'infinitely small' and instead use inscribed and circumscribed figures together with double reductio ad absurdum to prove equality (bounds method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: take both inscribed and circumscribed approximating figures, 'compress' them to coincide with the curvilinear figure, prove the target is neither greater nor less than the purported value. Examples: area of parabolic segment proven to be 4/3 of the triangle by iterative inscribed triangles and bounding argument; surface/volume derivations for spheres and segments using revolving polygons and limiting trig expressions, but justified by exhaustion rather than explicit limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for using conics vs algebraic reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to reduce a problem to a cubic equation or to solve it directly by geometric construction (conics) depends on the original figure and convenience: Apollonius often solved directly without bringing in the cubic; Archimedes introduced the cubic when no conic was present in the original figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding principle: if the problem's geometry already involves conics (or can naturally be handled by intersecting conics), a direct geometric solution is preferred (Apollonius 'compresses two steps into one'); if not, one may reduce to an algebraic cubic and treat it separately (Archimedes). Historical practice shows reduction to the cubic was sometimes unnecessary and even avoided when a direct conic construction was simpler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intersections of conics to solve cubic-type problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving cubic or related problems by constructing intersections of conics (e.g., parabola with rectangular hyperbola, ellipse with rectangular hyperbola) as demonstrated by Archimedes, Dionysodorus, Diocles, and Apollonius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and methods: Archimedes and Dionysodorus reduce sphere-segmentation problems to intersections involving parabola and rectangular hyperbola; Diocles uses an ellipse and a rectangular hyperbola to effect a division corresponding to a complete cubic; Apollonius determines normals by intersections of a rectangular hyperbola with the conic, sometimes yielding cubic equations. The chapter emphasizes that expressing the problem algebraically as a cubic was often avoided when the direct geometric intersection was available and more natural.
